home.bio: I'm a full-stack software engineer with over four years of experience building and running web platforms in production: React and Next.js on the front end, Node.js, GraphQL and C# on the back end, and AWS infrastructure with Terraform and Kubernetes. I led development on a civic engagement platform used by UK local councils, working with teams in the UK, Canada and Israel. I came to programming from Economics, through a thesis on Bitcoin, and graduated in software development from Trybe.

projects.title: projects.md
projects.heading: My projects
projects.intro: What I build on my own time, plus the projects I made while learning to program at the Trybe bootcamp. Everything public is on <github>GitHub</github>.

items.TFC: Football matches and standings API with JWT login, built in TypeScript with Express and Sequelize on MySQL. Runs in Docker and is covered by integration tests.
items.frontend-online-store: Started as a Trybe group project: an online store with real Mercado Livre products and prices in reais, categories, search, reviews and a cart. When Mercado Livre closed its public search in 2026, I wrote a Cloudflare Worker to keep it running. The Worker holds the API credentials and serves only my two storefronts, through Turnstile-verified sessions signed with HMAC. It validates every input before calling Mercado Livre and rate-limits each visitor.
items.shopping-cart: A single-page store in plain JavaScript with real Mercado Livre products and a receipt-style cart. It reads from the same Worker and passes the same Turnstile check before it gets any data.

projects.trybeHeading: Projects I started at Trybe, while learning to program
projects.trybeMore: The rest of my bootcamp work is collected in <collection>Trybe projects</collection>, where every app runs in the browser.

dead-mans-luck.name: Dead Man’s Luck
dead-mans-luck.about: No-limit Texas Hold’em at a lamp-lit table in an 1880s frontier saloon, against four characters with their own playing styles, lines and faces. The table is drawn with PixiJS on React and TypeScript. The bots only see what a player in their seat would see, a rule enforced by module boundaries and a lint check. It plays offline in the browser, in English and Portuguese, and an Android app is on the way.

ecclesia.name: Ecclesia
ecclesia.about: An interactive timeline of 2,000 years of Catholic and Christian history: over 6,700 events drawn on a WebGL canvas, with zoom, search, keyboard navigation, an accessible list view and shareable links. A TypeScript pipeline builds the dataset from Wikidata and Wikipedia.

crivo.name: Crivo
crivo.about: A Firefox and Chromium extension that uses an LLM to flag unsourced claims and logical fallacies in Brazilian news, highlighting the sentences right on the page. Backed by a Cloudflare Worker API with result caching and daily limits.

instagram.name: Hide Instagram Elements
instagram.about: A Firefox and Chrome extension that hides chosen parts of Instagram web, such as the feed, stories and suggestions, from a popup of toggles. Built with injected CSS so it survives Instagram re-rendering, and published on the Firefox Add-ons store.

experience.title: experience.md
experience.heading: Experience
experience.intro: Over four years as a full-stack software engineer at Westpoint, a UK software consultancy, building and maintaining web platforms and back-end systems in production. My work covers system architecture, production reliability, performance, zero-downtime migrations and merging platforms after an acquisition.

westpoint.title: Westpoint
westpoint.summary: A UK software engineering consultancy that places its engineers with client teams and builds projects of its own. I have worked on both, from new features to production support and cloud infrastructure.

civic.title: Civic engagement platform
civic.summary: A client project: an engagement platform UK local councils use to run public consultations and turn community feedback into evidence for their decisions. Councils build surveys and proposals, and residents answer them, comment and share their views on a map.
bullets: Built new features and integrations, fixed bugs and supported the platform in production

After the company was acquired in late 2025, kept the platform running and migrated customer accounts, users and consultations to the new owner’s platform with no downtime and no data lost, so councils moved over without disruption
Led the rework of the contribution flow, the journey residents follow to complete a survey
Built the map analytics section of the council dashboard from scratch, turning back-end data into charts and filters, and extended the charts on residents’ demographics and contributions
Developed and fixed the interactive maps, where residents drop pins, draw polygons and place custom SVG markers, with the geodata in PostGIS and GeoJSON, and made crash-prone map pages stable
Reworked the login system and migrated every user account to a new identity platform
Removed back-end bottlenecks in the Node.js services, including MongoDB indexes for slow queries
Fixed vulnerabilities found in the quarterly penetration tests
Ran on AWS EKS with Kubernetes, Helm and Docker, alongside Lambda, SQS, SNS and Step Functions
Worked daily with teams in the UK, Canada and Israel

internal.title: Internal projects
internal.summary: Westpoint’s own products. The stack changed from project to project.
bullets: Front ends in Next.js or React; back ends in C# / .NET or in Node.js with Express
Infrastructure as code with Terraform or AWS CDK, plus deployment pipelines and infrastructure automation
Serverless work on Lambda, API Gateway, SQS, SNS, Step Functions, S3, SES, DynamoDB, Route 53, ACM and CloudWatch
Moved AWS Lambda workloads into private VPC subnets, with Transit Gateway for private connectivity
Moved a whole platform from AWS to Azure, including its data from DynamoDB to Cosmos DB
Integrated third-party REST APIs with API keys and OAuth
